Sample.evidence_source: This section discusses "informants" and "participants" in a single study context, without indicating multiple distinct sub-studies.

Country.evidence_source: [page/4/Text/5] Only men attributed their suicidal act to spiritual forces. This could be understood in light of the Ghanaian culture.

Population.evidence_source: [page/3/Text/9] In spite of this perception and acknowledgement, however, our informants seemed to find no other way out of their predicament than to attempt to kill themselves. [page/4/Text/3] Against the backdrop of the acknowledgement of God as owner of life and death, some informants perceived their behaviour as a sin: "I see it as a sin. I know God is the answer to everything. Whenever you have patience, you always end up being successful. I did not have patience and I just sinned" (woman 2). Another participant also acknowledged that she should have relied on God as the suicidal act was a sin: "I feel it's not good … I should have taken it to God in prayer. I have sinned" (woman 1). [page/4/Text/4] We found a small group of men who felt compelled to (attempt to) kill themselves as a result of some spiritual or supernatural forces beyond their control, for example, "It was like some spirit entered me and made me do what I did … it's that small spirit that entered me and did not give me proper wisdom … " (man 2).

Type.evidence_source: [page/3/Text/9] In spite of this perception and acknowledgement, however, our informants seemed to find no other way out of their predicament than to attempt to kill themselves. [page/4/Text/5] The majority of the informants, however, understood and explained their suicidal act in accordance with the idea that God has superiority and ownership of life. We found two emerging themes as the informants' understandings and reactions to their suicidal act were either in accordance with God or in opposition to God.
